title: Capstone: Build a Helpdesk Resolution Agent
why: The exam explicitly tests judgment calls from production work — courses and question banks alone won't carry you through the scenario-based items. Building one real system that touches all 5 domains is the single highest-leverage thing you can do beyond the question bank.
overview: Build a small but real agentic helpdesk system: it receives a support request, looks up account/order context through tools, decides on an action (answer, refund, escalate), and is bounded by hard-coded gates so it can never take an action beyond its authority — regardless of how it's prompted. Scope it to a weekend project, not a product.
minimum_scope: A harness (a script or small service is enough — it doesn't need a UI) that calls the Claude API directly, not just Claude Code.
At least 2 tools with real (or realistically mocked) backends — e.g. an order-lookup tool and a refund-issuance tool.
At least one hard-coded gate that blocks a tool call regardless of the model's stated reasoning (e.g. a refund amount ceiling).
Structured output for at least one tool's result and for the agent's final decision (JSON, not free text).
A basic escalation path — some condition that hands off to "human review" instead of silently failing or looping forever.

phases.title: 1. Design the loop
tasks: Write out your own version of the 8-step loop (see Mental Model page) for this specific system before writing code.

Decide: single agent, or coordinator + subagents? Justify it — most helpdesk flows don't need multi-agent orchestration; add it only if there's a genuine reason (e.g. a separate research subagent for looking up policy docs).
Define your exit conditions explicitly: what ends the loop successfully, what forces an escalation, what's the max-turn ceiling.

phases.title: 2. Design the tools
tasks: Write tool schemas with clear, disambiguating descriptions (especially if you have two tools that could be confused, e.g. cancel_order vs. refund_order).
Design at least one dry-run/preview parameter for your highest-stakes tool and enforce that the harness actually surfaces it.
Design distinct error shapes for transient vs. permanent tool failures and confirm your harness handles each differently (retry vs. don't-retry).

phases.title: 3. Design the prompts and output
tasks: Define a strict JSON schema for the agent's final decision (e.g. {action, reasoning, confidence}).
Build a validation-retry loop: if the schema fails to parse, feed the specific error back and retry.
Add one semantic check beyond schema validity (e.g. if action is "refund", amount must be > 0 and <= the order total).

phases.title: 4. Wire in Claude Code for the build itself
tasks: Write a CLAUDE.md for this project describing its architecture and conventions (this doubles as practice for the domain and as real documentation).
Use plan mode for at least one non-trivial change (e.g. adding the escalation path) and compare the experience to direct execution on a trivial one.
Add at least one hook (e.g. run your test suite in PostToolUse after an edit) so enforcement doesn't rely on you remembering to run it.

phases.title: 5. Add reliability under load
tasks: Simulate a long conversation (10+ turns) and observe whether the agent's adherence to its own rules drifts — try re-anchoring the system prompt periodically and compare.
Add trimming/summarization for stale tool results once they're no longer relevant to the current turn.
Decide and document your clarify-vs-act policy for this specific domain (helpdesk decisions are usually low-cost-to-ask, high-cost-to-guess-wrong — does your agent's behavior reflect that?).

self_assessment_rubric.check: Can you point to the exact code line where your loop decides to stop vs. continue? Is there a hard max-turn ceiling?
If you fed your refund tool a wildly out-of-range amount, does a gate block it before the backend is touched — every time, not just usually?
Could a new teammate onboard onto this project using only your CLAUDE.md and repo, without you explaining it verbally?
Does your system correctly return null/no-action when it genuinely doesn't have enough information, instead of guessing?
After a deliberately long, meandering conversation, does the agent still remember and enforce its original constraints?

closing_note: You don't need to finish a polished product. The point is to have made the specific mistakes the exam asks about — a gate you forgot, a subagent context you didn't pass, a schema that parsed but was semantically wrong — because recognizing those failure modes from having hit them yourself is what the scenario-based questions are actually testing.
